title: Attribute Selectors: Targeting by Details 🔎
description: Select elements based on attribute presence, exact values, and partial matches.

slides.title: Why Attribute Selectors? 🧐
slides.content:
# Style Based on Attributes

Sometimes you need to target elements by their attributes without adding extra classes. Attribute selectors let you match:
- Presence of an attribute.
- Exact attribute value.
- Partial matches (contains, starts with, ends with).

Example: style all inputs with `type="text"` differently from `type="email"`.

slides.title: Presence and Exact Value ✔️
slides.content:
# The Basic Forms

- `[attr]` – element has the attribute (any value).
  ```css
  a[target] { /* <a target="_blank"> etc. */ }
  ```
- `[attr="value"]` – attribute exactly equals value.
  ```css
  input[type="text"] { border: 1px solid gray; }
  ```

Both are case‑sensitive by default (unless you add `i` at the end).

quizData.question: What does `[required]` select?

options.text: Any element that has the required attribute

quizData.explanation: `[required]` matches elements where the attribute is present, regardless of its value.

slides.title: Partial Match Attribute Selectors 🧩
Powerful Form Styling
slides.content: Attribute selectors can style form elements without extra classes:

quizData.question: Which selector targets links whose `href` contains the word 'progly'?
quizData.explanation: `*=` matches any occurrence of the substring within the attribute value.

slides.title: Case‑Insensitive Matching 🔠
Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Attribute Selectors Are Very Specific

They have the same specificity as a class (0,0,1,0). Use them wisely; they can make your CSS more expressive without cluttering HTML with classes.
